title: Eocene
description: Second epoch of the Paleogene Period
wiki_lead:
The Eocene (IPA:  EE-ə-seen, EE-oh-) is a geological epoch that began about 56 million years ago (Ma). It is the second epoch of the Paleogene Period in the modern Cenozoic Era. The end point of the Eocene is the Eocene-Oligocene transition (EOT), between 33.9 and 33.4 Ma. Precise boundaries between the epochs are sometimes given at 33.9 or 33.7 Ma.
The Eocene spans the time from the end of the Paleocene Epoch to the beginning of the Oligocene Epoch. The start of the Eocene is marked by a brief period in which the concentration of the carbon isotope 13C in the atmosphere was exceptionally low in comparison with the more common isotope 12C. The average temperature of Earth at the beginning of the Eocene was about 27 degrees Celsius. The end is set at a major extinction event called the Grande Coupure (the "Great Break" in continuity) or the Eocene–Oligocene extinction event, which may be related to the impact of one or more large bolides in Siberia and in what is now Chesapeake Bay. As with other geologic periods, the strata that define the start and end of the epoch are well identified, though their exact dates are slightly uncertain.

Etymology
The term "Eocene" is derived from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs), lit. 'dawn', and καινός (kainós), lit. 'new', as the epoch saw the dawn of recent, or modern, life.
Scottish geologist Charles Lyell (ignoring the Quaternary) divided the Tertiary Epoch into the Eocene, Miocene, Pliocene, and New Pliocene (Holocene) Periods in 1833. British geologist John Phillips proposed the Cenozoic in 1840 in place of the Tertiary, and Austrian paleontologist Moritz Hörnes introduced the Paleogene for the Eocene and Neogene for the Miocene and Pliocene in 1853. After decades of inconsistent usage, the newly formed International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS), in 1969, standardized stratigraphy based on the prevailing opinions in Europe: the Cenozoic Era subdivided into the Tertiary and Quaternary sub-eras, and the Tertiary subdivided into the Paleogene and Neogene periods. In 1978, the Paleogene was officially defined as the Paleocene, Eocene, and Oligocene epochs; and the Neogene as the Miocene and Pliocene epochs. In 1989, Tertiary and Quaternary were removed from the time scale due to the arbitrary nature of their boundary, but Quaternary was reinstated in 2009.


Geology


Boundaries
The Eocene is a dynamic epoch that represents global climatic transitions between two climatic extremes, transitioning from the hot house to the cold house. The beginning of the Eocene is marked by the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, a short period of intense warming and ocean acidification brought about by the release of carbon en masse into the atmosphere and ocean systems, which led to a mass extinction of 30–50% of benthic foraminifera (single-celled species which are used as bioindicators of the health of a marine ecosystem) –one of the largest of the Cenozoic. grok_lead: The Eocene Epoch, spanning approximately 56 to 33.9 million years ago, represents the second epoch of the Paleogene Period within the Cenozoic Era, a time characterized by warm global climates, the absence of polar ice caps, and the rapid diversification of mammals and modern plant lineages following the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. This epoch is divided into early (Ypresian), middle, and late stages, with the early Eocene marking one of the hottest intervals in Earth's history, featuring mean annual temperatures around 30Â°C and lush tropical forests extending to high latitudes. During the Eocene, Earth's climate was predominantly greenhouse-like, with high atmospheric carbon dioxide levels driving elevated temperatures and abundant precipitation, though a gradual cooling trend began in the middle Eocene due to tectonic changes such as the formation of the circum-Antarctic Current. A pivotal event was the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) around 55.5 million years ago, when global temperatures increased by 5 to 8Â°C over approximately 200,000 years, triggered by massive carbon releases that disrupted ocean chemistry and ecosystems. In polar regions like the Arctic, mean annual temperatures reached 13â15Â°C, supporting mixed conifer-hardwood forests with species such as pines, spruces, and walnuts, while the PETM further warmed these areas and shifted vegetation toward broad-leaved swamp forests including cypresses and palms. The Eocene saw profound evolutionary developments, particularly among mammals, which evolved from small, rodent-like forms in the early stages (typically under 10 kg) to larger, more diverse species by the late Eocene, including the first appearances of modern orders such as primates, artiodactyls (even-toed ungulates), perissodactyls (odd-toed ungulates), and early whales. Flowering plants (angiosperms) dominated terrestrial ecosystems, fostering dense forests that covered much of the continents, while avian groups diversified and insects adapted to the expanding floral resources. Marine life thrived in warm oceans, with the evolution of early cetaceans marking the transition of mammals to aquatic environments, though the late Eocene cooling and increased seasonality toward the Eocene-Oligocene boundary began favoring open savanna-like habitats over closed forests.
